title: Best Facial Recognition & Biometric Privacy Tools Compared
metaDescription: DeleteMe, Signal and infrared-blocking privacy glasses compared on photo protection, camera protection, data-broker removal, ease of use and cost.
intro: Facial recognition surveillance is everywhere - from stores to streets to social media. This comparison looks at three kinds of tool that cut your exposure: a data-removal service, an encrypted messenger and infrared-blocking glasses. None of them stops every kind of face scanning.

products.name: Privacy Glasses
products.tagline: Physical protection against infrared facial recognition cameras
products.pricing: About $50-$200, depending on brand and model
pros: Prescription lenses available from some makers
cons: May look conspicuous in some settings
Do little against ordinary daylight (visible-light) cameras

products.name: Signal
products.tagline: Encrypted messaging with photo protection features
pros: Face-blur tool that detects faces in photos before you send them
Open source; its encryption protocol has been independently analysed
cons: Requires contacts to also use Signal

products.name: DeleteMe
products.tagline: Paid service that removes your listings from people-search and data-broker sites
products.pricing: $129/year for one person; couple and family plans available
pros: Removes people-search listings, which can include photos
Quarterly reports on what it found and removed
cons: Costs more than doing the opt-outs yourself

verdict.summary: No single tool covers every kind of face scanning. On these five criteria DeleteMe scores highest: it removes people-search listings, which can include photos, and keeps monitoring for new ones, though it's a yearly subscription and can't remove photos posted elsewhere. Signal comes next: it's free and keeps the photos you share end-to-end encrypted, out of public view. Privacy glasses score lowest; they are the only physical option here, but they mainly affect infrared cameras, not ordinary daylight ones.

pro_tips: Layer your protection: limit who can see your photos online, remove people-search listings, and use physical options such as infrared-blocking glasses where cameras are the concern.
Regularly check your privacy settings on social media platforms and disable facial recognition features wherever possible.
Use Signal for sharing photos instead of regular text messages or social media to prevent images from being scraped.
Consider DeleteMe if you've been active online for years and want to clean up existing data broker profiles.
Stay informed about local facial recognition bans and support privacy legislation in your area to create systemic change.

faqs.question: Can facial recognition systems identify me if I wear sunglasses?
faqs.answer: Regular sunglasses provide minimal protection. Modern facial recognition systems can identify you using partial face features, ear shape, gait, and other biometric markers. Specialized privacy glasses that block infrared light work against infrared cameras, but do little against ordinary daylight cameras.

faqs.question: How does Clearview AI get my photos?
faqs.answer: Clearview AI collects publicly available photos from social media and other websites. How you browse doesn't change that, because the photos are taken from wherever they are posted publicly. Limiting who can see your photos, deleting old public ones and using any opt-out or deletion rights your local privacy law gives you all reduce your exposure.

faqs.question: Are there laws protecting me from facial recognition surveillance?
faqs.answer: Some cities and states have banned or restricted facial recognition use by government agencies. However, private companies generally have fewer restrictions. Check your local laws and support privacy legislation.

faqs.question: Do privacy tools work against all types of facial recognition?
faqs.answer: No single tool works against everything. Digital tools protect online, while physical tools protect against cameras. Combining multiple approaches provides the best protection against different surveillance methods.

faqs.question: Is it legal to use anti-surveillance tools?
faqs.answer: Yes, using privacy tools and anti-surveillance techniques is generally legal. However, some venues may have policies against face coverings. Always check local laws and venue rules.
